Wilder is a vigorous early twentieth-century American red currant selected for its long, well-filled clusters of large, bright red berries and reliably heavy cropping. It is a workhorse jelly and juice currant, valued more for productivity and fruit size than for fresh eating, since the flavor stays tart even at full ripeness. Like other red currants it fruits on spurs of two- and three-year-old wood, and it is best grown in regions with cool summers and consistent moisture.
sources: Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in fall in full sun; performs best where summers stay cool, struggling in regions with high heat and humidity.

directions: Plant dormant bushes in fall in full sun; this cultivar performs best where summers stay cool, struggling in regions with high heat and humidity. Gloire des Sablons is a distinctive French heirloom currant whose berries ripen with a marbled pink-and-cream streaked skin, midway in both color and sweetness between typical red and white currants. It is grown as much for its unusual coloring as for its genuinely good eating quality, being milder and less acidic than most red-fruited types. The self-fertile bush is vigorous, producing long, well-filled strigs in midsummer, and responds well to the same renewal pruning favored by other Ribes rubrum cultivars.
sources: Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide

Ben Alder is a late-season black currant from the Scottish Crop Research Institute's Ben breeding program, the same lineage that produced Ben Lomond, Ben Sarek, and Ben Nevis. It extends the black currant harvest window later into summer than most other Ben-series cultivars, bearing large, richly flavored berries on a vigorous, upright, cold-tolerant bush. Its late flowering helps it dodge spring frost damage that can cut yields in earlier-blooming currants, a useful trait in frost-prone regions.
sources: Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide

planting.note: Plant in full sun on well-drained, slightly acidic soil; self-infertile, so interplant with a different overlapping-bloom cultivar such as Indigo Gem or Aurora.

directions: Plant in full sun on well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and interplant with a different, overlapping-bloom cultivar such as Indigo Gem or Aurora for reliable pollination and fruit set, since this cultivar is self-infertile. Indigo Treat is a midseason haskap from the University of Saskatchewan breeding program, selected for a sweeter, less tart flavor than earlier releases like Indigo Gem, with large, elongated, deep-blue berries. The upright, extremely cold-hardy bush breaks dormancy early, so late spring frosts during bloom are the main risk to cropping rather than winter cold itself. Expect fruit to ripen a week or two after the earliest haskap cultivars.

planting.note: Grow in full sun in well-drained soil; pair with a similarly timed pollinizer such as Aurora or Borealis for adequate cross-pollination.

directions: Grow in full sun in well-drained soil, and provide consistent moisture during fruit development for the best size and flavor. Indigo Yum is one of the later-flowering cultivars in the University of Saskatchewan's Indigo series of haskaps, bred for a milder, sweeter flavor than earlier Indigo-series releases. Because its bloom period does not fully overlap with the earliest Indigo cultivars, it should be paired with a similarly timed pollinizer, such as Aurora or Borealis, to ensure adequate cross-pollination and fruit set. The compact, productive bush produces large, oblong blue berries with thin, tender skin well suited to fresh eating, jams, and baking.
